lessons.title: Emerging Technologies, Robotics and Artificial Intelligence
lessons.notes_html:
Emerging Technology

Emerging technology is generally referred to as a new technology — a technology that is newly developing and is expected to change the way we live and work. Important examples are Artificial Intelligence, robotics, blockchain, Virtual Reality and 5G. An older technology such as 3G is not an emerging technology.

Robotics

Robotics is the branch of technology that designs and builds robots. Robotics is replacing human efforts in many dangerous and repetitive jobs. The primary difficulties in robotics are that robots have no feelings or emotions, they are costly to design and maintain, they need a continuous power supply, and building robots that can safely work in every kind of environment is very difficult. Robots also cannot take decisions like humans in unexpected situations.

Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (AI) enables machines to act and think like humans. Applications of AI include self-driving cars, expert systems, chatbots, gaming, marketing, social media, natural language processing, machine vision and navigation control. AI is used in almost every field of life, such as healthcare, education, business and transport. A chatbot is an example of Artificial Intelligence.

Machine Learning

Machine Learning is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that enables a system to learn and improve itself from its experience without any user interference. A machine learning system improves itself with experience, just as humans learn from practice.

Computer Assisted Translation

CAT is also known as Computer Assisted Translation. Its main purpose is to help translators translate written and spoken text from one language to another quickly and accurately with the help of software programs. It increases the speed and consistency of translation work.

Key Points

  • Emerging technology means a new technology.
  • Machine Learning is a branch of AI that improves itself from experience.
  • A chatbot is an example of Artificial Intelligence.
  • CAT stands for Computer Assisted Translation.

mcqs.q: ______ is generally referred to as 'Emerging Technology'.
mcqs.why: Emerging technology is generally referred to as a new technology — one that is newly developing and expected to change the way we live and work.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of an emerging technology?
mcqs.why: 3G is an older, established mobile technology. Virtual Reality, Blockchain and Robotics are all new, fast-developing technologies, so they are emerging technologies.

mcqs.q: ______ is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that enables a system to learn and improve itself from its experience without any user interference.
mcqs.why: Machine Learning is the branch of Artificial Intelligence that enables a system to learn and improve itself from its own experience without any user interference.

mcqs.q: A chatbot is an example of:
mcqs.why: A chatbot is a program that talks with users like a human by understanding and answering their questions, which is an application of Artificial Intelligence.

mcqs.q: CAT is also known as:
mcqs.why: CAT stands for Computer Assisted Translation — software that helps translators translate written and spoken text quickly and accurately.

mcqs.q: An emerging technology is best described as a technology that is:
mcqs.why: Emerging technology is a new technology that is developing fast and bringing technical and social change — it is not an old, discontinued or 'absolute' technology.

mcqs.q: A machine learning system improves its performance by:
options: Being replaced by a new system every year
Needing user interference at every step
Learning from its experience and data
mcqs.why: Machine Learning enables a system to learn and improve itself from its experience, without any user interference — the system gets better as it processes more data.

mcqs.q: Robotics is increasingly used in industry because it:
options: Makes all products free of cost
Replaces human effort in dangerous and repetitive jobs
mcqs.why: Robotics is replacing human efforts in dangerous, difficult and repetitive work, although robots are costly, need continuous power and have no feelings or emotions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an application of Artificial Intelligence?
mcqs.why: Applications of AI include self-driving cars, expert systems, chatbots, gaming, marketing, machine vision and navigation control. The other options are old devices that do not use AI.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a primary difficulty in robotics?
options: Robots work without any power supply
Robots are very cheap to build
Robots have no feelings or emotions
Robots can decide like humans in every situation
mcqs.why: The difficulties in robotics include: robots have no feelings or emotions, they are costly to design and maintain, they need a continuous power supply, and they cannot take decisions like humans in unexpected situations.

lessons.title: Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality and 3D Technologies
lessons.notes_html:
Virtual Reality

Virtual Reality (VR) is a technology that creates a computer-generated imitation of the real world where people can interact in an apparently real or physical way. The user is fully immersed in the virtual environment through a VR headset (VR head-mounted display), which covers the eyes and shows a computer-generated 3D world, often together with headphones and hand controllers. VR is a 3D experience, not a 2D image.

Augmented Reality

Augmented Reality (AR) is a technology that overlays computer-generated images, sounds or information on a view of the real world. Unlike Virtual Reality, it does not replace the real world; it adds digital elements to it — for example, seeing furniture in your own room through a phone camera before buying it.

Difference Between VR and AR

Virtual Reality creates a completely computer-generated world; the user is fully immersed in it through a VR headset and cannot see the real surroundings. Augmented Reality keeps the user in the real world and only overlays digital images or information on it, usually through a phone or smart glasses. In short, VR replaces reality, while AR adds to reality. So VR and AR are not the same technology.

3D Imaging

3D imaging is used in medical imaging (CT and MRI scans), movies and video games, architecture and building design, manufacturing and product design, virtual reality, and in maps and weather forecasting. It helps us view objects with depth, just like real objects.

Holographic Imaging

Holographic imaging is a technique that creates a three-dimensional (3D) image, called a hologram, of an object using laser light. The image appears to float in the air and can be viewed from different angles without any special glasses. A simple hologram effect can be created at home with a smartphone and a transparent plastic pyramid (made from a CD case or clear sheet): place the inverted pyramid on the phone screen and play a hologram video; the four sides reflect the images and a 3D-like floating image appears inside the pyramid.

Key Points

  • VR replaces reality; AR adds digital elements to reality.
  • A VR headset is used to experience virtual reality.
  • A hologram is a 3D image created using laser light.

mcqs.q: ______ technology is a computer-generated imitation of the real world where people can interact in an apparently real or physical way.
mcqs.why: Virtual Reality is the computer-generated imitation of the real world in which people can interact in an apparently real or physical way, through a VR headset.

mcqs.q: Virtual Reality creates an environment that is:
mcqs.why: Virtual Reality is not a 2D image; it creates a three-dimensional (3D) computer-generated world in which the user feels present.

mcqs.q: The environment created by Virtual Reality feels ______ to the user.
options: Real and natural, although it is computer-generated
mcqs.why: Virtual Reality creates a natural-feeling environment: the imitation of the real world is so complete that the user interacts with it in an apparently real or physical way.

mcqs.q: Which device is used to experience virtual reality?
mcqs.why: A VR headset (VR head-mounted display) covers the eyes and shows the computer-generated 3D world, often with headphones and hand controllers, so the user feels present inside the virtual environment.

mcqs.q: Augmented Reality overlays digital images and information on:
options: A view of the real world
mcqs.why: Augmented Reality overlays computer-generated images, sounds or information on a view of the real world; it does not replace the real world, it adds digital elements to it.

mcqs.q: The main difference between VR and AR is that:
options: VR adds to reality, while AR replaces it
Both are used only for games
VR replaces reality, while AR adds to reality
mcqs.why: VR fully immerses the user in a computer-generated world and hides the real surroundings, while AR keeps the user in the real world and only overlays digital information on it.

mcqs.q: A hologram is a three-dimensional image created using:
mcqs.why: Holographic imaging creates a 3D image, called a hologram, of an object using laser light; the image appears to float in the air and can be viewed from different angles without special glasses.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an application of 3D imaging?
options: CT and MRI scans in medical imaging
mcqs.why: 3D imaging is used in medical imaging (CT and MRI scans), movies and video games, architecture, manufacturing, virtual reality, maps and weather forecasting.

mcqs.q: To create a simple hologram effect at home, we place a transparent plastic pyramid on:
options: A television that is switched off
A smartphone screen playing a hologram video
mcqs.why: Placing an inverted transparent plastic pyramid on a phone screen playing a hologram video makes the four sides reflect the images, and a 3D-like floating image appears inside the pyramid.

mcqs.q: An example of Augmented Reality is:
options: Seeing furniture in your own room through a phone camera before buying it
Wearing a VR headset to enter a game world
Listening to a song on the radio
mcqs.why: In this example the real room is still visible and only a digital image of the furniture is added to it through the phone camera — that is Augmented Reality.

lessons.title: Blockchain, 5G and Self-Driving Cars
lessons.notes_html:
Blockchain

Blockchain is a method of storing data that makes it difficult or impossible to change, hack or cheat the system. Data is stored in blocks, and each block is linked with the previous block, forming a chain. Once a transaction or file is recorded in a block, it cannot be modified. Copies of the chain are kept on many computers, so no single person controls it. Blockchain is used in digital currencies like Bitcoin, in banking, in record keeping and in secure data sharing.

Distributed Applications

Distributed applications are those which operate simultaneously on several different computers. Blockchain is a distributed system because copies of the same chain are kept and updated on many computers at the same time.

5G Technology

5G, the fifth generation of cellular technology, is better than previous generations because it gives a much higher data rate (estimated up to 20 Gbps), very low delay (latency), connects many more devices at the same time, and is more reliable. It supports self-driving cars, smart cities and the Internet of Things.

Self-Driving Cars

A self-driving car is also known as an autonomous vehicle (AV), a driverless car, or a robotic car. Such a car uses sensors, cameras, radar and GPS to observe its surroundings and to navigate without a human driver. It is not a manual vehicle, because no human driver drives it.

Key Points

  • In blockchain, recorded data cannot be modified.
  • The estimated data rate of 5G is up to 20 Gbps.
  • A self-driving car is also called an autonomous or driverless car.

mcqs.q: ______ applications are those which operate simultaneously on several different computers.
mcqs.why: Distributed applications are those which operate simultaneously on several different computers — for example, blockchain, whose copies are kept on many computers.

mcqs.q: In a blockchain system, the transaction or file recorded cannot be ______.
mcqs.why: Once a transaction or file is recorded in a block of the blockchain, it cannot be modified — this is what makes blockchain secure and trustworthy.

mcqs.q: The estimated data rate of 5G technology is ______.
mcqs.why: 5G gives a much higher data rate than previous generations, estimated up to 20 Gbps, with very low delay (latency).

mcqs.q: A self-driving car is also known as a ______ car.
mcqs.why: A self-driving car is also known as an autonomous vehicle (AV), a driverless car or a robotic car, because it navigates using sensors, cameras, radar and GPS without a human driver.

mcqs.q: A self-driving car navigates on the road:
options: With a driver holding the steering wheel at all times
Only when it is pushed by people
mcqs.why: A self-driving car is not a manual vehicle: it uses sensors, cameras, radar and GPS to observe its surroundings and navigate without a human driver.

mcqs.q: In blockchain, data is stored in ______ linked together to form a chain.
mcqs.why: In blockchain, data is stored in blocks, and each block is linked with the previous block, forming a chain that is very difficult to change or hack.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a use of blockchain?
mcqs.why: Blockchain is used in digital currencies like Bitcoin, in banking, in record keeping and in secure data sharing, because recorded data cannot be modified.

mcqs.q: A self-driving car observes its surroundings using:
mcqs.why: A self-driving car uses sensors, cameras, radar and GPS to observe its surroundings and to navigate without a human driver.

mcqs.q: 5G is better than previous generations because it provides:
options: Higher data rate and very low latency
mcqs.why: 5G gives a much higher data rate (up to 20 Gbps), very low delay, connects many more devices at the same time and is more reliable than previous generations.

mcqs.q: Copies of the blockchain are kept on:
options: Many computers at the same time
mcqs.why: Blockchain is a distributed system: copies of the chain are kept on many computers, so no single person controls it and the data stays secure.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Data Communication and Computer Networks

lessons.title: Data Communication and Types of Networks
lessons.notes_html:
Data Communication

Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through some transmission medium. The message is the information or data to be communicated, such as text, numbers, pictures or sound. An encoder converts the message into signals suitable for transmission, and a decoder converts the received signals back into the original message.

Why Computer Networks Are Necessary

Computer networks are necessary because they allow sharing of resources such as printers, files and internet connections, fast communication between people, sharing of data and software, and central control and backup of information. They save time, money and effort in offices, schools and homes.

LAN and WAN

A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small geographical area such as a room, building or office; the entire LAN is simple to operate and easy to control, and it is usually owned by one organization. A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a greater distance, operates citywide, nationwide or worldwide, and is made by connecting many LANs through communication devices such as PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) or satellite links. In a WAN, the computers are not physically connected to each other. A MAN covers a city-sized area, between LAN and WAN.

VPN and DNS

A VPN is a secured connection over the internet. A Domain Name Server (DNS) translates human-readable domain names (such as www.example.com) into IP addresses that computers use to locate each other on the internet; it directs web and email traffic to the correct server.

Packet Transmission and TCP/IP

In packet transmission, data is broken into small packets. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) divides the data into packets, numbers them, and at the receiving end reassembles them in order and requests re-sending of any missing packet. IP (Internet Protocol) adds the source and destination addresses and routes each packet across the network.

Internet of Things

The Internet of Things (IoT) connects everyday devices — lights, fans, refrigerators, watches and cars — to the internet so they can be controlled remotely and can exchange data. Because it makes homes and cities smarter and life more comfortable, IoT is spreading quickly and will become even more popular in the future.

Key Points

  • A LAN covers a small area; a WAN covers a large distance.
  • A VPN is a secured connection over the internet.
  • DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.

mcqs.q: The network with a small geographical area is called:
mcqs.why: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small geographical area such as a room, building or office, and is simple to operate and easy to control.

mcqs.q: In the ______ network, computers are not physically connected.
mcqs.why: In a WAN, distant networks are joined through communication links such as PSTN or satellite links, so the computers are not physically connected to each other.

mcqs.q: ______ is a secured connection over the internet.
mcqs.why: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secured connection over the internet that keeps the data safe while it travels.

mcqs.q: PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) or satellite links are ______ devices used for WAN.
mcqs.why: PSTN and satellite links are communication devices/links used to connect distant LANs together to form a WAN.

mcqs.q: A LAN is simple to operate and easy to control because it:
options: Covers a small area and is owned by one organization
mcqs.why: The entire LAN is simple to operate and easy to control because it covers a small geographical area, such as one office, and is usually owned by a single organization.

mcqs.q: A WAN covers a greater distance and operates:
mcqs.why: WAN covers a greater distance and operates citywide, nationwide or worldwide by connecting many LANs together.

mcqs.q: The device that converts the message into signals suitable for transmission is called an:
mcqs.why: An encoder converts the message into signals suitable for transmission, while a decoder converts the received signals back into the original message.

mcqs.q: In data communication, the 'message' is:
options: The information or data to be communicated
The computer at the receiving end
The power supply of the network
mcqs.why: The message is the information or data to be communicated, such as text, numbers, pictures or sound.

mcqs.q: The function of a Domain Name Server (DNS) is to:
options: Store all the websites of the world
Translate domain names into IP addresses
mcqs.why: A DNS translates human-readable domain names, such as www.example.com, into the IP addresses that computers use to locate each other on the internet.

mcqs.q: In packet transmission through the internet, TCP is responsible for:
options: Dividing data into numbered packets and reassembling them in order
mcqs.why: TCP divides the data into packets, numbers them, and at the receiving end reassembles them in order and requests re-sending of any missing packet; IP routes the packets using addresses.

lessons.title: Guided Transmission Media: Twisted Pair, Coaxial and Fiber Optic Cables
lessons.notes_html:
Twisted Pair Cable

A twisted pair cable is made by twisting two separate insulated copper wires together that run parallel to one another — not seven wires. Twisting reduces noise and interference. Advantages: it is cheap, easy to install and widely available, and is commonly used in telephone lines and LANs. Disadvantages: it has low bandwidth, is easily affected by noise and electromagnetic interference, and signals become weak over long distances, so it is suitable only for short distances.

Coaxial Cable

A coaxial cable is a guided transmission medium consisting of a central copper conductor surrounded by insulation, a metallic shield and an outer plastic jacket. Advantages: it carries data over larger distances than twisted pair, has higher bandwidth, and is less susceptible to noise and interference because of its shield; it is frequently used in cable television (CATV) networks. Disadvantages: it is more expensive and thicker/less flexible than twisted pair, installation is more difficult, and a fault in the cable can disturb the whole network.

Fiber Optic Cable

The basic elements of a fiber optic cable are: the core (thin glass or plastic fiber that carries light), the cladding (a layer around the core that reflects light back into the core), and the protective plastic coating/jacket that protects the fibers from electromagnetic interference, heat and cold. Optical fiber cable is thinner and lighter in weight than copper cable, so it can withstand more pressure than a copper cable.

Key Points

  • A twisted pair has two insulated copper wires twisted together.
  • A coaxial cable has a central conductor, insulation, a metallic shield and a jacket.
  • In fiber optic cable, the core carries light and the cladding reflects it back.

mcqs.q: Each twisted pair consists of ______ insulated copper wires twisted together.
mcqs.why: A twisted pair is made by twisting two separate insulated copper wires together; the twisting reduces noise and interference.

mcqs.q: An optical fiber cable is thinner and lighter than a copper cable, so it can:
options: Withstand more pressure than a copper cable
Only be used for telephone calls
mcqs.why: Optical Fiber Cable is thinner and lighter in weight, so it can withstand more pressure than a copper cable, and it carries data as light signals through its core.

mcqs.q: A coaxial cable is frequently used in:
mcqs.why: Coaxial cable is frequently used in cable television (CATV) networks because it can be cabled over larger distances than twisted-pair cable and carries signals with less interference.

mcqs.q: In a fiber optic cable, the part that carries the light is the:
mcqs.why: The core is the thin glass or plastic fiber at the centre of the cable that carries light; the cladding around it reflects the light back into the core.

mcqs.q: In a fiber optic cable, the cladding is the layer that:
options: Reflects light back into the core
Connects the cable to the computer
Gives electric power to the cable
mcqs.why: The cladding is a layer around the core that reflects light back into the core, keeping the signal travelling along the fiber.

mcqs.q: Twisting the two wires in a twisted pair cable helps to:
options: Increase the weight of the cable
Store more data in the cable
mcqs.why: The two insulated copper wires are twisted together because twisting reduces noise and electromagnetic interference in the signal.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of twisted pair cable?
options: Signals become weak over long distances
It is the most expensive cable
It cannot be used in LANs
It is very difficult to install
mcqs.why: Twisted pair has low bandwidth, is easily affected by noise, and its signals become weak over long distances, so it is suitable only for short distances — although it is cheap and easy to install.

mcqs.q: The metallic shield in a coaxial cable protects the signal from:
mcqs.why: The braided metallic shield around the central conductor makes the coaxial cable less susceptible to noise and interference than twisted pair cable.

mcqs.q: Compared with twisted pair, a coaxial cable can carry data:
options: Over larger distances with higher bandwidth
mcqs.why: Coaxial cable carries data over larger distances than twisted pair and has higher bandwidth, though it is more expensive and less flexible.

mcqs.q: The outer plastic jacket of a fiber optic cable protects the fibers from:
options: All kinds of data loss forever
mcqs.why: The protective plastic coating/jacket of a fiber optic cable protects the fibers from electromagnetic interference, heat and cold.

lessons.title: Wireless Transmission Media: Radio Waves, Microwaves, Wi-Fi and Li-Fi
lessons.notes_html:
Unguided (Wireless) Transmission Media

Unguided media transmit electromagnetic waves without using any physical medium; the waves travel through air or space. They are also called wireless transmission media. Their three categories are: (1) Radio waves — low-frequency waves that travel in all directions through open space; used in radio, television and cellular networks. (2) Microwaves — high-frequency waves that travel only in a straight line and need line-of-sight antennas; used in long-distance telephone communication, mobile phones and satellite links. (3) Infrared — very short-range waves used in remote controls and short-distance device communication; they cannot pass through walls.

Satellite Communication and GPS

Satellite communication uses satellites in space to send signals over very long distances. GPS (Global Positioning System) is a subcategory of satellite communication, used to find locations and directions.

Wi-Fi, Li-Fi and Bluetooth

Wi-Fi stands for Wireless Fidelity. A Wi-Fi network is an internet connection that is shared with multiple devices in a home or business via a wireless router, using radio waves. Li-Fi is a wireless optical networking technology that uses LEDs (light) for data transmission. Li-Fi can be much faster and more secure because light does not pass through walls, but it works only where light can reach; Wi-Fi covers a larger area and passes through walls and doors. Bluetooth is an important short-range (low-range) wireless communication system that lets nearby devices communicate with each other without cables.

Key Points

  • Unguided media send waves through air or space without any physical medium.
  • Microwaves travel only in a straight line.
  • Li-Fi uses LEDs; Wi-Fi uses radio waves.
  • Bluetooth works without cables over a short range.

mcqs.q: Li-Fi is a wireless optical networking technology that uses ______ for data transmission.
mcqs.why: Li-Fi uses light from LEDs for data transmission, while Wi-Fi uses radio waves; light does not pass through walls, which makes Li-Fi more secure but limited to where light can reach.

mcqs.q: An unguided transmission media transmits electromagnetic waves without using any ______ medium.
mcqs.why: Unguided media transmit electromagnetic waves through air or space without using any physical medium such as a cable — that is why they are called wireless media.

mcqs.q: ______ is a subcategory of satellite communication.
mcqs.why: GPS (Global Positioning System) is a subcategory of satellite communication; it uses satellites to find locations and directions.

mcqs.q: A ______ network is an internet connection that is shared with multiple devices in a home or business via a wireless router.
mcqs.why: A Wi-Fi network shares one internet connection with multiple devices in a home or business through a wireless router.

mcqs.q: Wi-Fi stands for:
mcqs.why: Wi-Fi stands for Wireless Fidelity; it uses radio waves to connect devices to a network without cables.

mcqs.q: Bluetooth is an important ______-range wireless communication system.
mcqs.why: Bluetooth is a short-range (low-range) wireless communication system used to connect nearby devices such as phones, headphones and computers.

mcqs.q: Bluetooth technology allows devices to communicate with each other:
mcqs.why: Bluetooth is a wireless technology — devices communicate using radio waves over a short range, not through cables.

mcqs.q: Microwaves travel:
mcqs.why: Microwaves travel only in a straight line and need line-of-sight antennas, unlike radio waves which travel in all directions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a category of unguided transmission media?
mcqs.why: The three categories of unguided media are radio waves, microwaves and infrared. Twisted pair, coaxial and fiber optic are guided (cabled) media.

mcqs.q: Li-Fi can be more secure than Wi-Fi because:
options: Light does not pass through walls
It works in total darkness only
mcqs.why: Light does not pass through walls, so a Li-Fi signal stays inside the room; Wi-Fi radio waves pass through walls and doors and cover a larger area, but can be picked up outside.

lessons.title: Workbook, Worksheet and the Excel Interface
lessons.notes_html:
MS Excel: Workbook and Worksheet

MS Excel is spreadsheet software. A workbook is the Excel file that typically contains one or more worksheets. A worksheet is a single sheet of rows and columns inside a workbook where data is entered; the intersection of a row and a column is called a cell. One workbook can hold many related worksheets, shown as sheet tabs at the bottom.

Components of the Excel Interface

  • Title Bar: shows the name of the workbook.
  • Ribbon: contains tabs and the icons (toolbars) for commands.
  • Formula Bar: shows the contents or formula of the active cell.
  • Name Box: shows the address of the active cell.
  • Worksheet area: a grid of rows (numbered) and columns (lettered) whose intersections form cells.
  • Sheet Tabs: for moving between worksheets.
  • Scroll Bars: for moving up/down and left/right.
  • Status Bar: at the bottom, shows information such as sum, average and count of selected cells, and the zoom slider — it is not used to display colours.

The Ribbon Tabs

The main Ribbon tabs in MS Excel are: File — opening, saving, printing and closing workbooks; Home — clipboard, font, alignment, number formats, styles and editing; Insert — tables, charts, pictures and symbols; Page Layout — page setup, margins, orientation and themes; Formulas — the function library, including all built-in functions; Data — sorting, filtering and data tools; Review — spelling, comments and sheet protection; View — workbook views, zoom and window options. Each tab groups related commands as icons on the ribbon.

Key Points

  • The intersection of a row and a column is called a cell.
  • A workbook contains one or more worksheets.
  • The Name Box shows the address of the active cell.

mcqs.q: The intersection of a row and a column in a worksheet is called a ______.
mcqs.why: A worksheet is a grid of rows and columns, and the intersection of one row and one column forms a cell, where data is entered.

mcqs.q: A ______ typically contains one or more worksheets.
mcqs.why: A workbook is the Excel file that typically contains one or more worksheets, shown as sheet tabs at the bottom of the window.

mcqs.q: MS Excel is a ______ software.
mcqs.why: MS Excel is spreadsheet software used to save and process data in rows and columns and to perform calculations with formulas and functions.

mcqs.q: The Status Bar in Excel is used to:
options: Show information such as sum, average and count of selected cells
mcqs.why: The Status Bar, at the bottom of the window, shows information such as the sum, average and count of the selected cells and the zoom slider — it is not used to display colours.

mcqs.q: The Ribbon in Excel:
options: Contains tabs with icons for commands
Shows the name of the workbook
mcqs.why: The Ribbon contains tabs such as File, Home, Insert and Formulas, and each tab groups related commands as icons (toolbars) on the ribbon.

mcqs.q: The address of the active cell is shown in the:
mcqs.why: The Name Box shows the address of the active cell, while the Formula Bar shows the contents or formula of that cell.

mcqs.q: The name of the workbook is shown on the:
mcqs.why: The Title Bar at the top of the Excel window shows the name of the workbook that is currently open.

mcqs.q: The contents or formula of the active cell are shown in the:
mcqs.why: The Formula Bar shows the contents or formula of the active cell, so the user can see and edit what is inside the cell.

mcqs.q: To move between the different worksheets of a workbook, we use the:
mcqs.why: Sheet Tabs at the bottom of the window are used for moving between the worksheets contained in one workbook.

mcqs.q: All of Excel's built-in functions are found in the function library on the ______ tab.
mcqs.why: The Formulas tab contains the function library, including all of Excel's built-in functions; the other tabs group different commands.

lessons.title: Formulas, Functions and Charts in Excel
lessons.notes_html:
Formulas and Functions

Every formula in Excel begins with an equal sign (=), followed by the calculation. Functions are predefined, built-in formulas: a function is a formula with a name. All of Excel's functions are located on the Ribbon's Formulas tab. Three built-in functions are: SUM, which adds the values in a range of cells, e.g. =SUM(A1:A5); AVERAGE, which finds the mean of values, e.g. =AVERAGE(A1:A5) — the AVERAGE function requires reference to the address of cells; and IF, which tests a condition and returns one value if true and another if false, e.g. =IF(A1>=50,"Pass","Fail"). Other examples are MAX, MIN and COUNT.

The IF Function

The IF function allows you to make logical comparisons between values. It is used to test if a certain condition in a worksheet is true or false, and it returns one result when the condition is true and another result when it is false.

A Worked Calculation

Marks of a student in five subjects are in cells B2:F2 (70, 80, 75, 90, 85). Total: type =SUM(B2:F2) — the result is 400. Average: type =AVERAGE(B2:F2) — the result is 80. Both functions take the cell range as their argument and calculate automatically when the values change.

Charts

Data may be represented in different formats like graphs and charts to understand data visually. Charts are also commonly known as graphs. To create a chart of a store's monthly sales: enter data in two columns (Month and Sales), select the data range including headings, click the Insert tab and choose a chart type such as Column Chart, then add a chart title and axis labels. The chart shows at a glance in which month sales were highest or lowest.

Key Points

  • Every Excel formula starts with the = sign.
  • Functions are built-in formulas with a name, found on the Formulas tab.
  • Charts are also commonly known as graphs.

Formatting in MS Excel

Formatting in MS Excel includes making text bold, italic or underlined, changing font size and colour, filling a cell with a background colour, applying borders, merging cells, aligning text, and using number formats such as currency, percentage and dates. So the background colour of a cell can be changed, and two or more cells can be merged into one. Formatting makes the worksheet clear, attractive and easy to read.

Resizing a Column

To resize a column, place the mouse pointer on the right border of the column header until it becomes a double-headed arrow, then drag it to the required width. Alternatively, double-click the border to auto-fit the column to its contents, or right-click the column header, choose Column Width, and type an exact value.

Lab Activity: Marks Table of 10 Students

Create columns: Name, Subject 1 to Subject 5, Total, Average. Enter marks for 10 students. In Total use =SUM(B2:F2) and in Average use =AVERAGE(B2:F2), then copy the formulas down for all students. Taking 40 as pass marks, check each subject cell; wherever a student's marks in a subject are below 40, select that student's name cell and apply red fill colour (Home tab > Fill Color > Red) to show the failure clearly.

Lab Activity: Class Data Chart

Collect class data (birthday month / favourite food) and make a two-column table: the answer choice (e.g. Jan, Feb, ... or a food item) in the left column and the number of students in the right column. Count the class responses and fill in the numbers. Select the table, then Insert > Chart (column or pie) to draw the graph. lessons.title: Introduction to Google Sheets
lessons.notes_html:
What is Google Sheets?

Google Sheets is a free, online, web-based spreadsheet application developed by Google. It is linked with a Google Account, runs in the browser without downloading or installation, and is used to save and process data in rows and columns and to perform calculations with formulas and functions. Google Sheets is available in 83 languages, and it was launched as part of the G Suite pack in 2006.

Why We Use Google Sheets

We use Google Sheets to organize data in rows and columns, perform calculations with formulas and functions, create charts, and share the sheet with others for real-time collaboration. Work is saved automatically online (on Google Drive), so it can be opened anywhere with an internet connection.

Applications of Google Sheets

Applications of Google Sheets include preparing budgets and accounts, maintaining marks sheets and attendance records, making lists and timetables, analyzing data with pivot tables, creating charts and graphs, and collaborative project work where many users edit the same sheet at the same time from different places. Google Sheets is a spreadsheet program — it is not used to write letters and memos.

Google Sheets vs Excel

Google Sheets is a free online web-based application by Google that runs in a browser and saves files on Google Drive (not OneDrive, which belongs to Microsoft). Excel is Microsoft's installed spreadsheet software that saves files on the computer (or OneDrive). Both can be used in offline mode. Sheets is best for sharing and real-time collaboration; Excel offers more advanced features and is better suited to large and complex work — for small volumes of data, either is easy to use.

What Makes Google Sheets Better for Teamwork

Google Sheets is free, needs no installation, saves work automatically, allows many people to edit the same sheet in real time, keeps a complete version history, and can be used on any device through a browser. These features make it better than Excel for teamwork and online work.

Key Points

  • Google Sheets is a free online spreadsheet app by Google.
  • It is available in 83 languages and was launched in 2006.
  • Files are saved on Google Drive, not OneDrive.

lessons.title: Working with Google Sheets: Selection, Formulas and Ranges
lessons.notes_html:
Creating New Sheets and Selecting Cells

Open the spreadsheet and click the '+' (Add Sheet) button at the bottom-left corner to add a new sheet tab; you can also use the shortcut key Shift + F11 to create new sheets. Right-click a sheet tab to rename, duplicate, move or delete a sheet. To select multiple cells, click the first cell and drag the mouse over the other cells, or click the first cell, hold Shift and click the last cell of the range; for non-adjacent cells, hold Ctrl and click each cell. Selecting a cell, selecting multiple cells and selecting a column are all selection operations. You can select the entire spreadsheet by pressing Ctrl+A. The Name Box displays the reference of which cell or range you have selected. The buttons you press to perform actions are known as commands, and you can change the font colour of any cell.

Formulas and Functions

A formula in Google Sheets is an expression used to do mathematical calculations; formulas always start with the equal sign (=) typed in the cell, followed by the calculation. The predefined formulas in Google Sheets are referred to as functions. Three examples: =A1+B1 (adds two cells), =SUM(A1:A5) (total of a range), =AVERAGE(A1:A5) (mean of a range). Note that the MAX function returns the maximum value in a range — the function that returns the minimum value is MIN. The Data Grid is the part that saves and processes data in columns and rows and allows you to do calculations. To fill out a whole row with a formula, enter the formula in the first cell (e.g. =A1+B1 in cell C1), then drag the small fill handle (the square at the cell's bottom-right corner) across the row; the formula is copied with automatically adjusted cell references.

Ranges

A range in Google Sheets is a group of cells selected together, identified by the reference of its first (top-left) cell and last (bottom-right) cell separated by a colon — e.g. A1:C5 means all cells from A1 to C5. Ranges are used in formulas and functions such as =SUM(A1:A10), in formatting many cells at once, in sorting and filtering, and in creating charts and pivot tables. A range can be a single row, a single column, or a rectangular block of rows and columns.

The Toolbar (Ribbon) in Google Sheets

The toolbar/ribbon area below the menu bar contains the buttons (commands) used to perform actions: undo/redo, print, zoom, number formats, font name and size, bold/italic, text and fill colour, borders, merge cells, alignment, text wrapping, inserting links, comments and charts, and filters. Above it, the menus — File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Data, Tools, Extensions and Help — group all commands by type.

Key Points

  • Shift + F11 creates a new sheet; Ctrl+A selects the entire spreadsheet.
  • Formulas always start with the = sign; predefined formulas are called functions.
  • A range is written with a colon, e.g. A1:C5.

lessons.title: Computational Thinking and Its Techniques
lessons.notes_html:
What is Computational Thinking?

Computational thinking (CT) is a problem-solving method that allows us to take a complex problem, understand what the problem is and develop possible solutions, so that the solution can be carried out by a person or a computer. It is important to learn because it helps us solve problems logically and step by step, and the same thinking is used in programming, science, business and daily life.

The Four Techniques

  • Decomposition: breaking a complex problem or system into smaller, more manageable parts, solving each part separately, and then combining the results to solve the whole problem.
  • Pattern Recognition: observing patterns, trends and regularities in data, along with looking for similarities among and within problems.
  • Abstraction: focusing only on the important details of a problem, while ignoring irrelevant information, so the problem becomes simpler to understand and solve.
  • Algorithm Design: developing a step-by-step approach for solving a problem.

Decomposition divides the problem; abstraction filters the information. Factoring problems are problems that can be broken down (factored) into smaller independent parts, where each part is solved separately and the partial results are then combined — for example, the total cost of a school trip can be factored into transport cost, food cost and ticket cost, each found separately and then added.

Pros and Cons of Computational Thinking

Pros: (1) It breaks difficult problems into simple parts, so solutions become clear and reliable. (2) Its solutions can be reused — the same pattern or algorithm can solve many similar problems, and can be given to a computer. Working on independent parts at the same time (concurrency) speeds up the solution; it does not slow it down. Cons: (1) Thinking in strict steps is not possible for every problem; some problems (like the halting problem) are undecidable. (2) It takes time and practice to decompose a problem correctly, and over-simplifying (too much abstraction) can hide an important detail.

Key Points

  • CT = Computational Thinking.
  • Decomposition breaks a problem into parts; abstraction keeps only important details.
  • Pattern recognition finds similarities; algorithm design gives the step-by-step solution.

lessons.title: Algorithms, Pseudocode and Flowcharts
lessons.notes_html:
Algorithms

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. Rules for writing an algorithm: begin with the word Start and end with Stop; write each step in a separate line; steps must be clear, simple and in a definite order; the algorithm must take input, process it and produce output; it must finish in a finite number of steps; and it should be general enough to solve the problem for different inputs. Repeating an action again and again is called iteration. Algorithms are used everywhere in real life: recipes for cooking, instructions to reach a place, withdrawing money from an ATM, search engines, navigation apps, and washing machines and lifts following fixed step-by-step procedures.

Pseudocode

Pseudocode is an informal, plain-language description of an algorithm that uses simple English statements together with programming-like keywords such as INPUT, IF, THEN, ELSE, WHILE and PRINT. It is not a real programming language; it helps the programmer plan the logic before writing actual code. Pseudocode is often better than a flowchart because it is quicker to write and easier to change, can describe long and complex logic in a small space, and converts easily into program code — while flowcharts are better for beginners and for showing decisions visually.

Flowcharts

A flowchart is a diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols connected by flow lines (arrows). The oval represents Start/Stop — there can be only one start and one stop symbol in a flowchart. The rectangle shows a process, the diamond shows a decision, and the parallelogram shows input/output. The flow lines (arrows), not the diamond, show the direction of the flow of data and instructions, and flow lines can cross each other. Like an algorithm, certain rules must be followed while drawing a flowchart. Nesting is the placement of one object within another object.

Example: Boiling Water

Algorithm: Step 1: Start. Step 2: Take a kettle/pot. Step 3: Fill it with water. Step 4: Place it on the stove and turn on the heat. Step 5: Wait until the water boils (bubbles and steam appear). Step 6: Turn off the stove. Step 7: Stop. Flowchart (in words): Oval 'Start' → Rectangle 'Fill pot with water' → Rectangle 'Heat the water' → Diamond 'Is water boiling?' — if No, loop back to heating/waiting; if Yes → Rectangle 'Turn off the stove' → Oval 'Stop'.

The Halting Problem

The halting problem asks: can we write a program that, given any other program and its input, always decides whether that program will eventually stop (halt) or run forever? It is undecidable. Proof (by contradiction): suppose such a decider H exists. Build a program P that does the opposite of what H predicts for P itself: if H says P halts, P loops forever; if H says P loops, P halts. Both cases give a contradiction, so H cannot exist.

Key Points

  • An algorithm begins with Start and ends with Stop; each step is on a separate line.
  • In a flowchart: oval = Start/Stop, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, parallelogram = input/output.
  • The halting problem is undecidable.

lessons.title: Problem-Solving Activities with Computational Thinking
lessons.notes_html:
Tic-Tac-Toe Strategy

Ali's strategy to win at tic-tac-toe: (1) take the centre square first, as it gives the most winning lines; (2) take corners rather than edges; (3) always block the opponent when the opponent has two marks in a row; (4) try to create a 'fork' — two possible winning lines at the same time — because the opponent can block only one of them. This is pattern recognition and planning ahead.

Flowchart Activity: Bilal's Bus or Subway

Bilal takes the bus to school if it is before 7 a.m., otherwise he takes the subway. Flowchart (in words): Oval 'Start' → Process 'Bilal leaves home and looks at his watch' → Input 'Read the time' → Diamond 'Is the time before 7 a.m.?' — Yes branch → Process 'Take the bus'; No branch → Process 'Take the subway' → both branches join → Process 'Reach school' → Oval 'Stop'.

Pseudocode Drawing and Examples

Following the pseudocode 'move forward 100 steps, turn right 90 degrees' repeated 4 times draws a square: each pair of instructions draws one side and turns one corner; after four sides and four right turns (360 degrees in total) the pen returns to the starting point. Examples of pseudocode: (1) Add two numbers: INPUT A, B; SUM = A + B; PRINT SUM. (2) Make tea: BOIL water; ADD tea leaves; ADD sugar and milk; SIMMER 2 minutes; POUR and SERVE. (3) Find the larger number: INPUT A, B; IF A > B THEN PRINT A ELSE PRINT B.

Sudoku and Logic Puzzles

The 4 × 4 Sudoku (given: row 1 has 1 in column 2; row 2 has 2 in column 3; row 3 has 3 in column 2; row 4 has 1 in column 3) solves to — Row 1: 2, 1, 3, 4. Row 2: 3, 4, 2, 1. Row 3: 1, 3, 4, 2. Row 4: 4, 2, 1, 3. Every row, column and 2 × 2 box contains 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once. In the cake-baking competition (clues: Mariam was not first; Usman was not last; Neha was placed next to neither Mariam nor Usman; Ali scored better than Mariam), the result is: 1st Neha, 2nd Ali, 3rd Usman, 4th Mariam.

River-Crossing Puzzles

Wolf, goat and cabbage (the boat carries the man plus one item): (1) Take the goat across; leave it on the far bank. (2) Return alone. (3) Take the wolf across. (4) Bring the goat back. (5) Take the cabbage across (wolf and cabbage are safe together). (6) Return alone. (7) Take the goat across again. The fox, chicken and grain puzzle is solved in exactly the same way, taking the chicken first.

Muddy City and the Bridges of Königsberg

The Muddy City problem — pave enough streets so everyone can travel between all houses only on paved roads at the least cost — is solved by building a minimum spanning tree greedily: repeatedly choose the cheapest street that connects a house not yet connected, never pave a street that forms a complete loop, and stop when all houses are connected (47 counters in the book's map). For Königsberg's seven bridges: representing each land mass as a vertex and each bridge as an edge, a walk using every edge exactly once is possible only with 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices; all four land masses have an odd number of bridges (3, 3, 3 and 5), so such a walk is impossible.

Choosing the Best Algorithm: Linear vs Binary Search

To find a name in a class list: linear search checks names one by one from the start — simple, but slow for a long list. Binary search (the list must be sorted) checks the middle name and then searches only the half where the name can be, repeating until found. Binary search is the best algorithm here because it halves the remaining list at each step, so it needs far fewer comparisons for large lists.

Key Points

  • The pseudocode drawing activity produces a square.
  • In river-crossing puzzles, take the middle item (goat/chicken) across first.
  • Binary search is faster than linear search on a sorted list.

mcqs.q: The Muddy City problem is solved at the least cost by building a:
options: List of all houses in order
mcqs.why: Greedily paving the cheapest street that connects a not-yet-connected house — and never completing a loop — builds a minimum spanning tree that connects all houses with the fewest stones.

mcqs.why: A street that forms a complete loop is never paved, because one street of the loop can be removed without disconnecting anyone — paving it would waste stones.

mcqs.q: A walk crossing each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once is:
options: Impossible, because all four land masses have an odd number of bridges
Possible if we start on an island
mcqs.why: An Eulerian trail needs 0 or 2 vertices of odd degree; in Königsberg all four land masses have odd degrees (3, 3, 3 and 5), so no route can cross each bridge exactly once.

mcqs.q: Binary search is better than linear search for a long list because it:
options: Needs the list to be unsorted
Halves the remaining list at each step
mcqs.why: Binary search checks the middle name and discards half the list each time, so it needs far fewer comparisons than linear search, which checks names one by one.

mcqs.q: In the solved 4 × 4 Sudoku, the first row is:
mcqs.why: The solved grid is Row 1: 2, 1, 3, 4; Row 2: 3, 4, 2, 1; Row 3: 1, 3, 4, 2; Row 4: 4, 2, 1, 3 — every row, column and 2 × 2 box contains 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once, matching the given clues.

lessons.title: Scratch Basics: Sprites, Scripts and Block Categories
lessons.notes_html:
What Is in Every Scratch Project?

Every Scratch project contains a Sprite (a character or object that performs actions), the Stage (the background area where the project runs) and a Script (the set of joined blocks that tells the sprite what to do). The blocks serve as commands that can be joined together like puzzle pieces to build a script.

The Block Categories

  • Motion: used for moving sprites around the stage — blocks such as 'move 10 steps', 'turn 15 degrees', 'go to x: y:' and 'if on edge, bounce', which control the position and direction of a sprite.
  • Looks: used for animating sprites, giving them speech bubbles, and changing their size and appearance — blocks such as 'say Hello!', 'switch costume to', 'change size by' and 'set size to %'.
  • Sound: used for playing recordings or musical notes — blocks such as 'play sound', 'play drum' and 'play note'.
  • Events and Control: Events blocks (such as 'when green flag clicked' and 'when space key pressed') describe what happens when something occurs and start scripts; Control blocks (such as 'repeat', 'forever', 'wait' and 'if...then') make parts of the program repeat or run only under a condition.
  • Sensing: used to test whether your sprite is touching another sprite or another colour, or to get information about other sprites — blocks such as 'touching...?', 'touching colour...?', 'ask... and wait' and 'mouse x/y'.
  • Operators: used for Maths, random numbers, and doing things to text — arithmetic blocks (+, −, ×, ÷), 'pick random', comparison blocks (>, <, =) and text blocks such as 'join' and 'length of'.

Backdrops

A program can have more than one backdrop. Click the Stage and then the Backdrops tab, and use the 'Choose a Backdrop' button (or paint/upload) to add more backdrops. To change the backdrop during the program, use the Looks blocks 'switch backdrop to ...' or 'next backdrop' — for example, to start a new level of a game when the player reaches a certain score.

Why Scratch Is Good for Beginners

Scratch is good for animation, games and storytelling because programs are made by joining colourful blocks like puzzle pieces, so there are no typing or syntax errors. It has ready-made sprites, costumes, sounds and backdrops, and blocks for motion, looks and events, so animations, games and interactive stories can be created quickly and the results are seen immediately on the stage.

Key Points

  • Every Scratch project has a sprite, a stage and a script.
  • Motion blocks move sprites; Looks blocks change appearance; Sensing blocks test touching.
  • Blocks are commands that join together like puzzle pieces.

mcqs.why: Blocks serve as commands that can be joined together like puzzle pieces to build a script for the sprite.

mcqs.why: The Motion category contains blocks such as 'move 10 steps' and 'turn 15 degrees' that move sprites around the stage.

mcqs.why: The Looks category contains blocks such as 'say Hello!', 'switch costume to' and 'change size by', which control how a sprite looks and what it says.

mcqs.q: Blocks such as 'play sound', 'play drum' and 'play note' belong to the ______ category.
mcqs.why: The Sound category is used for playing recordings or musical notes, adding music and sound effects to a project.

mcqs.q: To test whether a sprite is touching another sprite or a colour, we use the ______ category.
mcqs.why: The Sensing category contains blocks such as 'touching...?' and 'touching colour...?', which let a sprite sense its surroundings.

mcqs.q: 'Pick random', arithmetic blocks and 'join' text blocks are found in the ______ category.
mcqs.why: The Operators category is used for Maths, random numbers and doing things to text — it holds arithmetic, comparison and text blocks such as 'join' and 'length of'.

mcqs.q: To change the backdrop during a running program, we use:
mcqs.why: Backdrops are changed during the program with the Looks blocks 'switch backdrop to ...' or 'next backdrop' — for example, to start a new level of a game.

mcqs.q: Scratch is considered good for beginners because:
options: It has no sprites or sounds
Programs are made by joining blocks, so there are no typing or syntax errors
mcqs.why: In Scratch, programs are made by joining colourful blocks like puzzle pieces, so beginners face no typing or syntax errors and see results immediately on the stage.

mcqs.q: The area where a Scratch project runs and is watched is called the:
mcqs.why: The Stage is the background area where the project runs; sprites perform their actions on the stage.

lessons.title: Programming Concepts in Scratch: Loops, Conditions, Variables and Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Programming and Program

Programming is the process or activity of writing instructions for a computer — designing, coding, testing and improving them. A program is the finished product: a set of instructions (code) written in a programming language that the computer follows to perform a task. In short, programming is the work; the program is the result of that work.

Elements of Programming

Four elements are enough to build almost any program: (1) Variables — named storage for values that can change, e.g. score and lives. (2) Sequence — instructions executed one after another in order; the blocks in a script form a sequence of commands. (3) Selection (conditionals) — 'if...then...else' blocks choose different actions depending on whether a Boolean expression is true or false. (4) Iteration (loops) — 'repeat', 'forever' and 'repeat until' blocks repeat actions.

Variables and Boolean Expressions

A variable is a named storage place in a program that holds a value which can change while the program runs — for example score, lives or speed in a game. In Scratch, variables are created from the Variables category, and blocks can set, change and show their values. A Boolean expression is an expression that is either true or false — for example 'score > 10' or 'touching the edge?'. In Scratch, Boolean expressions are the pointed (hexagonal) blocks found mostly in Sensing and Operators; they fit inside the condition slots of blocks like 'if...then' and 'repeat until', which is how you can identify them.

Loops

A loop is a programming construct that repeats a set of instructions again and again, instead of writing them many times. In Scratch: 'repeat 10' runs the enclosed blocks exactly 10 times; 'forever' runs them endlessly until the program stops; 'repeat until <condition>' runs them until the condition becomes true — so a loop and a condition are combined in the 'repeat until' block. Example: to draw a square, repeat 4 times: 'move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees'.

Functions and My Blocks

In programming, a function is a block of code that you may reuse repeatedly rather than having to write it out several times. In Scratch, a function is some block that performs some task, and new blocks are made from the My Blocks category. Nesting means combining two structured programming constructs in a way that one construct is inside the other. The Text to Speech feature is used to convert text into speech in Scratch.

Key Points

  • A Boolean expression is either true or false.
  • 'Repeat until' combines a loop with a condition.
  • New custom blocks are made in My Blocks; functions are reused code.

mcqs.q: A loop and a ______ are combined in the 'repeat until' block.
mcqs.why: The 'repeat until' block combines a loop with a condition: the enclosed blocks keep repeating until the condition becomes true.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is used to make a new block in Scratch?
mcqs.why: New custom blocks (functions) are made from the My Blocks category, so a task can be defined once and reused.

mcqs.q: In programming, a Boolean expression is an expression that is either true or ______.
mcqs.why: A Boolean expression has only two possible values: true or false — for example 'score > 10' is either true or false.

mcqs.q: In programming, a function is a block of code that you may ______ repeatedly rather than having to write it out several times.
mcqs.why: A function groups instructions under one name so they can be reused repeatedly instead of being written out several times.

mcqs.q: A ______, in the context of Scratch, is some block that performs some task.
mcqs.why: In Scratch, a function is a block that performs some task; making such a block in My Blocks lets the whole task run with a single block.

mcqs.q: ______ is used to convert the text into speech in Scratch.
mcqs.why: The Text to Speech feature converts written text into spoken words in a Scratch project.

mcqs.q: Combining two programming constructs so that one construct is inside the other is called:
mcqs.why: Nesting indicates that two structured programming constructs are combined in a way that one construct is inside the other — for example, an 'if' block inside a 'repeat' block.

mcqs.q: In a game, the player's score that keeps changing while the program runs is stored in a:
mcqs.why: A variable is a named storage place that holds a value which can change while the program runs — score, lives and speed are common game variables.

mcqs.q: Boolean blocks in Scratch can be identified because they are:
options: Pointed (hexagonal) blocks that fit into condition slots
Found only in the Sound category
mcqs.why: Boolean expressions are the pointed (hexagonal) blocks found mostly in Sensing and Operators; they fit inside condition slots of blocks like 'if...then' and 'repeat until'.

mcqs.q: The 'forever' loop runs its enclosed blocks:
options: Only when the sprite is clicked
mcqs.why: A 'forever' loop runs the enclosed blocks endlessly until the program stops — for example, a game keeps checking 'if the sprite touches the edge' for the whole game.

lessons.title: Scratch Projects, Cloning and Coding Tasks
lessons.notes_html:
Events and Control in Projects

The Events category starts scripts when something happens — for example 'when green flag clicked', 'when a key is pressed', or 'when this sprite is clicked' — and sends/receives broadcast messages between sprites. The Control category controls the flow of a script: 'wait' pauses it, 'repeat' and 'forever' loop blocks, 'if...then' and 'if...then...else' run blocks only when a condition is true, and cloning blocks create and delete copies of a sprite.

Cloning Blocks

The three main blocks for cloning in Scratch (Control category) are: (1) 'create clone of myself' — makes an exact copy of the sprite while the program runs. (2) 'when I start as a clone' — the script under this block runs for each new clone, giving it its own action. (3) 'delete this clone' — removes the clone when its work is finished, so too many copies do not fill the stage.

Reading a Script

Consider the script: when green flag clicked → switch to costume costume2 → set size to 100% → turn 15 degrees → move 10 steps → if on edge, bounce. It means: when the green flag is clicked, the sprite changes into its second costume (costume2), its size is set to 100%, it turns 15 degrees clockwise, moves forward 10 steps, and if it touches the edge of the stage it bounces back (turns around to face the opposite direction).

Why Write Functions?

A function groups a sequence of instructions under one name (e.g. 'jump'), so the whole action can be run by simply calling the function wherever it is needed. Advantages: the code is shorter and tidier; the same instructions are not written again and again; a mistake can be corrected in one place only; and the main script becomes easier to read and understand. Writing the instructions directly everywhere would duplicate code and make the program hard to change.

Coding Tasks

Calculator: Ask 'Enter first number' and store in variable A; ask 'Enter second number' and store in B; ask 'Choose: 1 sum, 2 difference, 3 product, 4 quotient'. Use if/else: if choice = 1, say A + B; if 2, say A − B; if 3, say A × B; if 4, say A ÷ B. Trampoline jump: when the space key is pressed (or forever, if touching the trampoline), change the costume to the 'jumping' costume, change y by +10 repeatedly until the peak, then change y by −10 until the sprite lands back on the trampoline, and switch back to the normal costume.

Limits of Scratch

Limits of Scratch include: it is designed for learning, so it is slower and less powerful than text-based languages for very large or complex programs; projects run inside the Scratch environment/website and cannot easily become standalone professional software; advanced topics such as working with files, databases and real hardware are limited; and very detailed graphics or 3D games are difficult to build.

Key Points

  • Cloning uses three blocks: create clone, when I start as a clone, delete this clone.
  • Functions save repetition and make code easier to correct.
  • Scratch is designed for learning, so it has limits for very large programs.

mcqs.q: How many main blocks are used for cloning in Scratch?
mcqs.why: The three main cloning blocks are 'create clone of myself', 'when I start as a clone' and 'delete this clone' — all in the Control category.

mcqs.q: The block 'create clone of myself' is used to:
options: Make an exact copy of the sprite while the program runs
mcqs.why: 'Create clone of myself' makes an exact copy of the sprite while the program runs; the clone then follows the script under 'when I start as a clone'.

options: Too many copies do not fill the stage
mcqs.why: 'Delete this clone' removes the clone when its work is finished, so too many copies do not fill the stage and slow the project.

mcqs.why: The script sets the size to 100%, then turns the sprite 15 degrees clockwise and moves it 10 steps; the numbers 10 and 100 belong to the move and size blocks.

options: Turn around and face the opposite direction at the stage edge
mcqs.why: If the sprite touches the edge of the stage, it bounces back — it turns around to face the opposite direction and keeps moving.

mcqs.why: The calculator asks for the first number and stores it in variable A, asks for the second number and stores it in B, then uses if/else to say A+B, A−B, A×B or A÷B according to the user's choice.
